entries.title: Resort Connected to Jim Justice Ordered to Pay $52 Million for Defaulting on Pandemic Loan
entries.summary: The Greenbrier Resort’s finances have been mired in legal clashes.
entries.content:
A federal judge ordered The Greenbrier Resort, partially owned by the family of West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice, to repay $35 million in Main Street Lending Program funding, plus $17 million in interest, for defaulting on the loan.

The ruling on the unpaid pandemic loan is another chapter in the Justice family’s nearly 20-year ownership of the storied resort, which has also been mired in what the billionaire lawmaker recently described as “a highly complex legal dispute” over the resort’s future.

In this case, the loan was provided by First Guaranty Bank in Louisiana and chaired by businessman Marshall T. Reynolds, a Huntington, West Virginia, native. First Guaranty sued over the loan, which had been delinquent since December 2023, in a case that began in Louisiana before moving to the Southern District of West Virginia.

The judge, in an opinion Thursday, said there was no question Greenbrier defaulted and rejected the resort’s arguments why judgment should not be entered now.

The Greenbrier didn’t dispute that it missed payment, but contended the bank unfairly rejected a February 2025 proposal to push full repayment to the end of 2026, the opinion says.

The bank’s CEO testified that the Federal Reserve turned down the request by phone, although that was never put in writing, and nothing in the loan documents required the bank to agree to the proposal to extend the repayment date, the judge wrote.

Justice purchased the then-struggling historic resort in 2009, and handed day-to-day control to his daughter Jill when elected governor of West Virginia in 2016. Since the purchase, the resort has struggled with increasing debt. In late March 2026, the Rowling family, which owns Omni Hotels, paid $289 million to pay off the resort's first-lien debt.

The Justices sued, alleging Carter Bank and TRT Holdings, the parent company of Omni Hotels and Resorts, conspired to force them out. Omni’s subsidiary asked a federal court to appoint a receiver.

Earlier this year, the Justices announced an agreement with Kennedy Lewis Investment Management in an effort to bring financial stability to the resort, which ended the feud with Omni. The firm took 51% ownership of the resort company for a reported $500 million, leaving the Justice family with 49%.

The Greenbrier Resort, Kennedy Lewis Investment Management and the Justice family did not immediately return The Washington Sun’s inquiries.

A Government Accountability Office report in June found that 70% of the Main Street program’s loans had been fully repaid. The initiative was established in the CARES Act and was one of 13 emergency lending programs in response to COVID-19. The loans were supposed to be paid back by early January 2026.

The resort itself is over 100 years old, and sits on 11,000 acres of land in southern West Virginia. The resort also housed an underground emergency shelter for the United States Congress built during the Cold War before it was decommissioned after The Washington Post exposed it in 1992.

entries.title: Sabres Beat Capitals, 6-3, In Fourth Straight Loss
entries.summary: Alex Ovechkin broke a tie with longtime teammate Nicklas Backstrom for Washington's career lead in assists with his 763rd.
entries.content:
By Noah Trister

Rasmus Dahlin and Beck Malenstyn scored 25 seconds apart in the first period to chase Logan Thompson, and the Buffalo Sabres sent Washington to its fourth straight loss, beating the Capitals 6-3 on Thursday night.

Jack Quinn scored twice — once into an empty net — and Zach Benson and Tage Thompson also scored for the Sabres. Buffalo converted on five of its 13 shots in the first two periods. Alex Tuch, Ryan Leonard and Boone Jenner scored Washington, which has fallen to .500 after entering the season with lofty expectations.

Alex Ovechkin broke a tie with longtime teammate Nicklas Backstrom for Washington's career lead in assists with his 763rd.

The Capitals have allowed at least five goals in four straight games and six of their last eight. On Wednesday it took them only two periods to do so. Thompson allowed three goals on five shots before being yanked in favor of Charlie Lindgren.

It was the second time in his last six starts Thompson was pulled early.

After Quinn opened the scoring, Dahlin entered the zone on a power play, and when Thompson overplayed him a bit to the near post, the Buffalo defenseman swooped behind the net and wrapped the puck into the vacated other side.

Malenstyn made it 3-0 and Thompson's night was done.

Tuch scored again against his former team. He had two goals against Buffalo, including the winner in overtime, in a game last month.

It was 4-1 after one Thursday, and Tage Thompson scored on the power play near the end of the second. Leonard scored to cap a dominant stretch on the power play for Washington in the third, then Jenner poked the puck in with 10:16 remaining after Buffalo goalie Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen seemed unaware it was loose.

Ovechkin received an assist on Jenner's goal, having passed to him in the neutral zone before Jenner dumped the puck toward the net, followed it and poked it in.

With neither team playing particularly well of late, Washington's Tom Wilson and Buffalo's Sam Carrick dropped the gloves right off the opening faceoff. Both were given fighting majors just one second into the game.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Senators Pass Permitting Reform. Will It Survive the House?
entries.summary: An amendment process fell apart after objections from Democrats over a push to restrict data center development on public lands.
entries.content:
The Senate passed a permitting reform bill with bipartisan support Thursday evening, advancing legislation that would reshape the way major energy projects are built.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 passed 62-33.

Almost every Republican in the Senate voted in favor of the bill, which supporters say would cut red tape that holds back new power plants, factories and other infrastructure projects. Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Josh Hawley of Missouri were the two Republicans in opposition. Fifteen Democrats and Independents also supported it, saying the legislation would lead the country into a clean energy future and address climate-warming emissions. Both sides of the aisle argue the bill addresses affordability issues and would help reduce power bills.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), one of the bill’s core negotiators, told reporters she was “thrilled beyond words” after the bill passed and that the deal between four lawmakers from vastly different backgrounds was “monumentally legacy-setting for the country.” 

“I think we’ve got great momentum going into the House,” she said.

The legislation has been endorsed by trade groups from the American Petroleum Institute to the Solar Energy Industries Association and by several labor unions, including the AFL-CIO. It has splintered the environmental movement, though, with longtime climate hawks such as Al Gore and Bill McKibben speaking out against it, while it has attracted support from the advocacy groups Citizens’ Climate Lobby and Evergreen Action.

Several Senate Democrats dropped their support for the bill in recent days, expressing concerns over its effects on tribal sovereignty and changes to longstanding environmental laws like the Clean Water Act. They also grew concerned that it could be used to “lock in” fossil fuel development during the last two years of the Trump administration.

Senators spent Wednesday evening and Thursday negotiating an amendment process, which fell apart over demands from Oregon Democrats Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley. Merkley objected to the process itself, while Wyden was pushing for the inclusion of an amendment that would ban data centers on public lands.

Ultimately, Merkley blocked a vote on a bipartisan amendment from the bill’s sponsors that was meant to address concerns over tribal consultation and landowners’ compensation for transmission projects.

Late into the night on Thursday after the passage of the bill, Sen. Brian Schatz and Sen. Mike Lee, a core Republican negotiator of the bill, continued to push for the adoption of the bipartisan amendment as Merkley stood firm.

Lee accused Merkley of attempting to “sow fear, uncertainty and doubt, and put the bill in a position of vulnerability on the House side.”

Merkley said he blocked the amendment because of opposition to the permitting bill from tribes in the Northwest, and continued to push for other amendments that addressed data center concerns.

President Donald Trump has expressed his support for the bill. Its final hurdle is in the House, where both Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries have indicated their support.

Efforts to amend the bill could derail its path forward, after months of negotiations between a bipartisan group of four senators culminated in a delicate deal.

Rep. Eric Burlison (R-Missouri) said he has concerns that the bill could lead to more cases of eminent domain being used in his district to build more transmission lines.

“My local concerns are, what it’s gonna do to farmers in Missouri to have a 300-foot tower being forced on their property and being given, basically, a pittance, so that California and Chicago can have more electricity,” he said.

Republicans are also worried about opening the door to more offshore wind projects and new clean energy subsidies, Burlison said. But ultimately, he said, there is “a lot of good” in the bill, calling House passage “achievable, but not a certainty.”

Democrats may continue advocating for further protections for the National Historic Preservation Act and environmental laws.

“I’m concerned about the Clean Water Act and the impact on tribal communities,” said Rep. Paul Tonko of New York, who sits on the Energy and Commerce Committee and said Democrats are split over whether to support the legislation in its current form.

Rep. Scott Peters (D-California), who supports the bill, said he would be open to changes, but it would be difficult for the House to make amendments in the short period of time left before the end of the session.

“I’m not sure how much, first of all, flexibility, but also institutional capacity we’re going to have to make amendments here,” he said. “We’re kind of up against the end of the clock.”

Peters added that the House has had input on the front end, saying he has met regularly with chief Senate negotiators.

Several Democrats have pushed to table permitting reform until next year when they’ll have majorities in the House and Senate. But Peters said waiting would be counterproductive.

“It lowers costs, it lowers emissions, we should pass it,” he said.
